q: European rules put a floor under the bottling strength of vodka. Where does it sit?
exp: The United States sets its floor at forty percent, which is why some vodkas are bottled differently for each market. European rules also make a vodka distilled from anything other than cereals or potatoes name its raw material on the label.

q: A juniper-flavoured spirit from the Low Countries is built on a distillate of malted grain, and is sold as jonge or oude according to how much of that distillate it carries. Name it.
exp: Oude and jonge describe style rather than age, and the malt wine base is what makes the spirit read closer to a light whisky than to a London Dry. Its protected geographical indication covers the Netherlands, Belgium and small parts of France and Germany.

q: After juniper, one seed appears in more gin recipes than any other, bringing lemon peel and a sage-like warmth with it. Name it.
exp: The seed is rich in linalool, which reads as citrus and lavender and dovetails with the pine and pepper of juniper rather than sitting beside it. Angelica root is the third of the standard trio and works as a fixative, binding the lighter aromatics together.

q: Absinthe's early twentieth-century ban was blamed on a compound in wormwood that was later shown to be present in only tiny amounts. Name that compound.
exp: Analysis of surviving pre-ban bottles found it at levels far too low to cause the effects laid at its door; strength, cheap adulteration and simple volume explain the rest. European law now caps it in bitter spirits at thirty-five milligrams per litre, which most absinthe never approached anyway.

q: A French aperitif takes its anise character mainly from star anise and liquorice rather than from wormwood, and is poured one part to five of water. Name it.
exp: It appeared after absinthe was banned and stayed on after absinthe returned, because it is a different drink rather than a substitute. Liquorice supplies most of the sweetness, and at forty percent and above it is the water that turns it into a long aperitif rather than a shot.

q: A bottle of sweet vermouth has stood open on the back bar since the spring. What has happened to it, and what should have been done?
opts: It has thrown a deposit, and an open bottle should be decanted before it goes cloudy
It has refermented, and an open bottle should be kept sealed and warm to prevent that
It has oxidised, and an open bottle belongs in the refrigerator for a few weeks at most
Nothing at all, since fortification keeps an open bottle stable for a year on the bar
exp: Vermouth is wine at around sixteen percent, well short of a Port's nineteen to twenty-two, and no amount of sugar keeps air out of an opened bottle, so it browns and flattens like any other wine. A Martini built on tired vermouth is among the commonest faults on a bar and the cheapest of all to fix.

q: No aromatised wine may be sold as vermouth unless one particular botanical is present, and the German name for that plant is where the word vermouth came from. Name the plant.
exp: Wermut is the German, and Artemisia species remain the signature bitter of the category. The rest of the recipe is wide open: a vermouth may carry anything from citrus peel and cinchona to vanilla and rhubarb, but without the Artemisia it is merely an aromatised wine.

q: Vermouth is a wine before it is anything else, and European law fixes the band of alcoholic strength it must sit inside. What is the lower limit of that band?
accept: fourteen and a half per cent
exp: The band runs from there to twenty-two percent, and at least three quarters of the finished drink has to be wine. Below the floor it is not an aromatised wine at all, and above the ceiling it has become a bitter liqueur.

q: One style of vermouth carries a geographical indication tying it to a northern Italian city and the region around it. Name that indication.
exp: The wine must be Italian and the production must happen in Piedmont, with the Superiore tier adding that the Artemisia itself be grown there. Turin is where the commercial category began in the eighteenth century, which is why the aromatised wine trade and the Italian bitters trade grew up in the same city.

q: A family of French aperitif wines takes its name from the bark that bitters it. Name the family.
exp: Cinchona bark supplies quinine, and these drinks were sold as a tonic against malaria long before anyone thought of them as an aperitif. Lillet, Dubonnet and Byrrh are the surviving names, and all of them are built on wine rather than on spirit.

q: Suze and Salers draw their bitterness from the root of a yellow alpine flower rather than from cinchona or wormwood. Name that plant.
exp: The roots are dug from mountain pasture, take decades to reach a useful size and are protected in some areas as a result. The same root bitters much of the Italian aperitivo family alongside citrus peel, and it is why those drinks taste earthy rather than merely sweet.

q: An order comes in for a drink of spirit, vermouth and bitters and nothing else, and the bartender reaches for a mixing glass rather than a shaker. What is that choice protecting?
opts: Clarity and a heavier texture, since there is nothing in the glass to emulsify
The bitters, whose aromatics break apart under agitation
The strength, since shaking drives off alcohol as the drink warms
The temperature, since a shaker cannot chill a drink as far as stirring can
exp: Shaking aerates and clouds, which suits a drink carrying citrus, egg or dairy and ruins one made only of spirits. Both methods chill and dilute; stirring simply does it more slowly and leaves the texture heavier.

q: The earliest printed definition of a cocktail, from 1806, names a spirit, sugar, water and one thing more. What is that fourth element?
exp: That definition, printed in a New York newspaper, is why the Old Fashioned is described as the original cocktail: it is exactly those four elements and nothing else. Everything with a name of its own came later, as ingredients were added to that frame.

q: Roughly a quarter of the liquid in a properly made stirred drink was never poured out of a bottle. Where did it come from?
exp: Water is an ingredient in every cocktail whether the recipe lists it or not, which is why the same ratios taste different stirred for ten seconds and stirred for thirty. Serving a stirred drink short of dilution leaves it hot, closed and unbalanced.

q: Rye, sugar, Peychaud's bitters and a rinse of an anise spirit make a New Orleans drink served with no ice in the glass. Name it.
exp: The glass is chilled and rinsed with absinthe or a pastis, and the drink itself is built separately and strained in. It began on Cognac and moved to rye once phylloxera cut the brandy supply, which is why recipes for both survive.

q: A spirit and a carbonated mixer over ice in a tall glass, with no citrus and no sugar added, belong to which family?
exp: Length is the point: the mixer supplies most of the volume, so the drink is judged on how much soda and how much ice rather than on ounces of spirit. Add citrus and sugar and it becomes a Collins, and shake that same mixture before the soda goes in and it becomes a fizz.
